title: God prays (Berakhot 7a)
hook: God's own prayer: may My mercy overcome My anger
tomorrow: can a person bless God? one high priest did.

segments.voice: Yesterday, God's tefillin: the binding goes both ways, and God carries us. The next page goes further still. God prays.

Someone says something at dinner, and the heat is in your face before you've decided anything. Half a second, and the sharp reply is loaded. Berakhot 7a pictures God knowing that moment, and having a prayer for it. In the Talmud's words, paraphrased: may it be My will that My mercy overcome My anger.
screen: `THE HEAT IN YOUR FACE.` → `THE SHARP REPLY, LOADED.` → `MAY MY MERCY OVERCOME MY ANGER.`

segments.voice: The page asks: how do we know God prays? From Isaiah, where God promises to make people joyful in My house of prayer. Not their house of prayer. Mine. So what does God pray? In Rav's name: may it be My will that My mercy conquer My anger, that My mercy prevail over My other ways, that I deal with My children with mercy, and go beyond the strict letter of the law for them. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: in the Talmud, God's prayer isn't for anything out there. It's about God's own temper. Now the debate, and it's an old one. Read it as Maimonides did: God has no body and no moods. Anger and mercy here are images, the Torah speaking in human language, and the prayer is a model held up for us. If God, so to speak, prays for mercy to win, so can we. Read it as the kabbalists did: mercy and strict judgment are real forces in how God meets the world, and the prayer shows them in tension, with mercy asked to lead. On that reading, human prayer and kindness can strengthen the side of mercy. One reading says the picture is for us. The other says the picture is real, and we're part of it. Both land in the same place: mercy over anger.

segments.voice: Think of one person likely to annoy you before tomorrow. Picture the exact moment the heat rises, and plan one merciful move for it: a slower breath, a softer first word, a question instead of a verdict. Rehearse it once in your mind, then hold it there for the rest of the sit.

howItsDone: Jewish prayer often appeals to God's mercy; in the penitential prayers before and during the High Holy Days, congregations recite the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy from Exodus 34 together.

chat.meaning: Berakhot 7a gives God's own prayer: may My mercy overcome My anger. The anger is real; mercy is asked to win.

Isaiah.meaning: a prophet whose book is in the Hebrew Bible

Maimonides.meaning: a medieval Jewish philosopher and legal scholar

kabbalists.meaning: teachers of Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition

Rav.meaning: a leading sage of the Talmud in Babylonia

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 7a (how do we know God prays; Rav Zutra bar Tuvia in Rav's name: may My mercy conquer My anger)
Isaiah 56:7 (joyful in My house of prayer)
Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed I:26 and Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:8–12 (God has no body; the Torah speaks in human language)
Kabbalistic readings of the divine attributes of mercy (chesed, rachamim) and judgment (din), e.g. the Zohar
